analysis.title: 10 Charts We're Talking About
key_insights: Cross-asset movers on a standardized basis show three competing cross-currents for risk markets: the AI hardware/infrastructure debate after the midterm results, weakness in energy prices, and a hotter than expected CPI that pressures the Fed toward more and faster hikes.
Winners in the standardized move ranking are the USD against oil exporters and safe havens. Losers are the more levered pockets of credit and front-end USD rates.

Hyperscalers look well positioned. Controllers of existing power and computing capacity gain leverage as new supply gets harder to build, and independent model developers and cloud intermediaries depend on access to that infrastructure. Owners can keep renting capacity externally or allocate more to their own models.

The neocloud complex is not equally well positioned. Citing Chamath Palihapitiya, operators that own land, power and shell have real leverage even in trouble, while operators holding only leases are middlemen in a business model that requires operational perfection.
Pressure on neoclouds may be compounded by weakness in NVDA, which was seen as the 'central bank of AI'.

GS analyst Jim Schneider draws an Apple 2011 analogy for NVDA: Apple de-rated from ~17X to ~12X NTM P/E over ~18 months around Steve Jobs' leave and death, traded as low as ~9X in 2013, then recovered to ~15X. He expects the market to search for the right NVDA multiple until leadership and business momentum are clearer.
Schneider says NVDA's current price likely represents favorable risk/reward given the ~80% EPS growth GS expects.

A NY Times poll taken before the midterms pushes back on the idea that voters focus on data center construction, but 'economy' ranks highest as the most important issue. The author argues the economy and AI-led infrastructure buildout are closely linked.
GS economists estimate wealth effects added more than 0.4pp to annualized consumption growth in 2026 as equities rose in H1. With home prices roughly flat, next year's impulse depends on equities.

Trump's post on 12 Nov reinforces the status quo and the maintenance of a blockade. The Dec 11 government spending deadline (including military) is the next political milestone, with a risk that Democrats seek to address the Iran war in those negotiations.
Bond bulls want the Fed to look through the hot CPI prints because energy prices are lower. Further Middle East escalation, or no resolution, may limit the Fed's ability to do so.

GS economists expect inflation to be meaningfully lower by end 2027, but think the recent prints will lead most FOMC participants to signal a third hike in the December dot plot. A firmer January inflation report would make delivering it the path of least resistance, even if the energy shock appears over by then.
GS added a third 25bp hike to its forecast in March 2027 and left the terminal fed funds forecast unchanged at 3.25-3.5%.

FX options desk charts (Praneet Shah) tie the themes together. If the conflict is a binding constraint on the Fed and shows better signs in the coming months, the bottom right quadrant unlocks. The author expects dispersion within the winners, tilted toward currencies with more pristine balance sheets.
